findings.title: Response construction and encoding block the event loop
findings.description: After the database work returns, the async handler builds every Pydantic row and serializes the full response synchronously. At the supported 75,000-row ceiling, this can involve tens of megabytes of data; the load test measures a ceiling-sized trades request at about one second. That CPU work blocks the event loop and delays other requests. Move the CPU-heavy response construction and encoding off the event loop, or otherwise ensure the large-response path does not block it.

findings.title: The count guard and fetch can observe different database snapshots
findings.description: The count and fetch are separate statements. With the default `READ COMMITTED` isolation, inserts committed between them can be visible to the fetch but not the count. The route then returns all fetched rows without rechecking the ceiling, so a request admitted at the limit can return substantially more than the configured maximum. Use a consistent snapshot for both reads, or another approach that preserves the all-or-refuse contract under concurrent writes.

findings.title: The filtered-tape flag can accompany returned trades
findings.description: The route fetches stored trades without considering the current exclusion setting, then sets `tape_filtered` from that setting. Because the exclusion is applied during collection and this route does not remove previously stored rows, a category that is now excluded can have both `tape_filtered: true` and a non-empty `trades` list. That conflicts with the response model’s description that `true` means no trades are stored by policy. Clarify the field’s meaning or make the response behavior consistent with that contract.
